screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Rehabilitation & Return to Sport queue positions 25-36.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Return to play and performance after primary ACL reconstruction in American football players - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review included 17 studies of American football players after primary ACL reconstruction. Return to play was 67.2% (1249/1859), mean return time was 11.6 months, and most included performance comparisons found larger postinjury declines than in controls.
records.limitations: The included studies were heterogeneous in players, outcomes, controls, and definitions of return and performance; many did not separate isolated reconstruction from concomitant procedures. Most evidence concerned professional football and observational comparisons.
records.synthesisCaution: Use these figures for sport-specific expectation setting, not as an individual prognosis or a clearance timeline; position, competition level, preinjury performance, concomitant injury, rehabilitation progress, and context matter.

records.sourceFile: Effects of Far-Infrared Radiation-Lamp Therapy on Recovery From Simulated Soccer Match Running Activities in Elite Soccer Players.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-four elite female soccer players were assigned to far-infrared lamp or sham therapy while completing six daily 90-minute simulated-match running tests. Relative to sham, the therapy group had smaller decrements in knee-extensor torque, countermovement jump, and Yo-Yo performance, lower soreness and creatine kinase, and earlier return toward baseline.
records.limitations: The small parallel study used simulated running rather than competition, studied only young elite women, and paired repeated treatment with an unusually demanding six-day protocol. Blinding credibility, clinical relevance, and effects beyond the observed recovery window remain uncertain.
records.synthesisCaution: This is one tightly controlled recovery experiment, not evidence that far-infrared therapy is required after matches or accelerates tissue healing; assess cost, feasibility, athlete response, and established recovery fundamentals.

records.sourceFile: High Return to Competition Rate After On-Field Rehabilitation in Competitive Male Soccer Players After ACL Reconstruction - GPS Tracking in 100 Consecutive Cases.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This case series followed 100 male 11-a-side soccer players through a five-stage, criteria-based on-field ACL rehabilitation programme. Ninety-seven had at least nine months of follow-up; 84% returned to competition (100% professional, 80% amateur), 10% sustained ACL reinjury, and final-stage external load approximated team-training demands but remained below match-play demands.
records.limitations: There was no comparison rehabilitation pathway, return outcomes came from follow-up questionnaire data, and professional and amateur players differed in exposure and workload. The sample was male soccer players at one specialist programme, so the high return rate cannot be attributed to GPS targets or the programme alone.
records.synthesisCaution: Use GPS to document graded field exposure and identify the gap to team and match demands, but do not treat a final-stage load percentage or programme completion as a stand-alone ACL clearance criterion.

records.sourceFile: Practice Patterns and Return-to-SportsTiming of National Football League Head Team Physicians for ACL Reconstruction.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: All 32 NFL head team orthopaedic surgeons completed a practice survey. Thirty-one reported ipsilateral bone-patellar tendon-bone autograft for primary reconstruction, mean return-to-sport timing was nine months with none allowing return before seven months, and all but one used functional testing in return decisions.
records.limitations: This was a descriptive survey of surgeons rather than athlete outcomes; answers may not represent actual care or team-wide decisions and cannot compare grafts, testing batteries, reinjury, or performance. Findings apply to an elite NFL setting.
records.synthesisCaution: Survey consensus describes current practice patterns, not a validated universal ACL protocol or proof that a specific graft, seven-month minimum, or functional test battery produces safe return.

records.sourceFile: Return to sport after surgical   treatment of Lisfranc injuries in athletes - A retrospective case series.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In a retrospective single-surgeon series of ligamentous Lisfranc injuries treated with open reduction and screw fixation, 10 athletes provided follow-up. Eight returned to sport at a mean 29.4 weeks, reported 87% of preinjury function, and six of nine reported occasional sport pain.
records.limitations: The study was very small, retrospective, and limited to selected 18- to 40-year-old recreational or competitive athletes receiving one procedure and surgeon's care. There was no nonoperative or alternative-fixation comparison, and subjective follow-up outcomes do not establish readiness or long-term joint health.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the result to frame that return may be possible but residual symptoms are common; surgical choice, tissue status, strength, foot function, sport demands, and individual progression still govern return decisions.

records.sourceFile: Cervical and Lumbar Disk Replacement in Athletes - Is It Safe to Return to Play - A systematic review of the scientific literature and lay press.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This PRISMA review found 10 scientific reports of total disk replacement in athletes: 53 cervical and 51 lumbar cases. Reported professional and semiprofessional athletes generally returned without reported complications, but only 14 professional contact-sport athletes across scientific reports and lay press were identified.
records.limitations: The evidence comprised small retrospective cohorts and case reports with highly selected athletes, sparse contact-sport exposure, variable procedures and follow-up, and supplemental lay-press reporting. Successful reported return is vulnerable to publication and selection bias.
records.synthesisCaution: Do not infer that disk replacement is broadly safe for collision sport from these sparse cases; specialist spine evaluation, imaging, neurological status, procedure details, risk tolerance, and shared decision-making remain decisive.

records.sourceFile: Groin pain in athletes and non-interventional rehabilitative treatment - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This review searched six sources through March 2017 and found randomized trials suggesting active treatment improved clinical signs of athletic groin pain versus passive treatment; multimodal treatment was associated with faster return to sport than active treatment alone. The authors described an integrated approach involving active and passive treatment, pain assessment, running progression, and sport-specific exercise.
records.limitations: The authors judged the evidence poor and could not issue practice guidelines. Groin diagnoses, interventions, doses, outcomes, and study quality were heterogeneous, so the review cannot identify a best treatment algorithm or apply one programme to every groin presentation.
records.synthesisCaution: First clarify the pain classification and competing pathology, then tailor loading and running progression; do not equate the review's broad multimodal description with a validated universal protocol.

records.sourceFile: High Rate of Return to Sport for Athletes Undergoing Articular Cartilage Restoration Procedures for the Knee - A Systematic Review of Contemporary Studies.pdf
records.exclusionReason: The local PDF text identifies a different article: a 2022 professional-soccer fixture-congestion study by Pinheiro et al. It does not match the queued cartilage-restoration title, so the assigned source identity fails closed.

records.sourceFile: Lower extremity return to sport testing - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review screened 19,189 records and analyzed 114 studies of lower-extremity return-to-sport testing. Eighty-five percent addressed knee pathology and 82% ACL reconstruction; isokinetic dynamometry was the most common test (73%), while hip and ankle evidence was sparse and no standardized clearance criterion emerged.
records.limitations: The review was dominated by ACL and knee studies, with substantial variation in injuries, tests, thresholds, and outcomes. It maps the literature rather than validating one battery's ability to reduce reinjury across joints or sports.
records.synthesisCaution: Use joint-specific strength, functional, movement, and patient-reported measures as part of a context-specific battery; neither a frequently used test nor limb symmetry alone establishes safe return.

records.sourceFile: Team Physician Consensus Statement - Return to Sport-Return to Play and the Team Physician - A Team Physician Consensus Statement - 2023 Update.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This team-physician consensus update defines return as a continuum from participation through sport to performance. It emphasizes an ongoing, context-dependent, athlete-centered shared decision process led by the team physician that weighs health, sport risk, performance demands, and athlete values while protecting athletes from coercion.
records.limitations: This is expert consensus rather than an injury-specific outcome study. It does not supply validated universal tests, thresholds, timelines, or outcome probabilities, and legal, staffing, and governance context vary across organizations.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the statement to structure accountable shared decisions and documentation, not to replace injury-specific assessment or to transfer a consensus process into a single automatic clearance rule.

records.sourceFile: Topical glyceryl trinitrate for the treatment of tendinopathies- a systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review identified 10 randomized trials of topical glyceryl trinitrate for rotator-cuff, wrist-extensor, Achilles, and patellar tendinopathy. Compared with placebo, short-term pain improvement had poor evidence; midterm satisfaction and asymptomatic daily activity had strong evidence, range and strength moderate evidence, and headaches were more frequent with glyceryl trinitrate.
records.limitations: Trials were few and heterogeneous in tendon, chronicity, dose, cointervention, comparator, outcome, and quality; evidence was not athlete- or return-to-sport-specific. The review did not establish optimal dosing, safety in all athletes, or superiority to progressive loading.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat topical glyceryl trinitrate, if medically appropriate, as a possible adjunct rather than a substitute for diagnosis and progressive tendon loading; account for headaches, contraindications, interactions, and sport-specific exposure.

records.sourceFile: Meniscus tears in elite athletes - Treatment considerations, clinical outcomes, and return to play.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This narrative review concludes that partial meniscectomy can permit quicker return, whereas repair is emphasized for anatomically repairable tears because it preserves native meniscus and may mitigate later cartilage damage; reported return rates and return to preinjury level can be similar. Meniscal allograft transplantation is described as a salvage option with promising but variable elite-sport outcomes.
records.limitations: The review is narrative and draws on heterogeneous, mostly observational sport-specific reports with varying tear patterns, procedures, definitions of return, and follow-up. It cannot establish one superior option or timeline for an individual athlete.
records.synthesisCaution: Base treatment and return planning on tear pattern and location, tissue repairability, concomitant injury, knee stability, symptoms, capacity, season context, and long-term joint goals—not speed of return alone.
